screens.title: Cisco DNA Center and SD-WAN Automation APIs
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will explore two complementary Cisco controllers and their automation APIs: DNA Center, which centers intent-based networking across campus and branch, and vManage, the SD‑WAN controller for overlay automation. We will learn what APIs are available, how token-based authentication works in practice, and how Python scripts can obtain tokens and query device inventories. You will also see how vManage exposes similar automation surfaces for SD‑WAN tasks like onboarding, templates, and monitoring. Understanding these controllers matters because they let you move from repetitive CLI work to repeatable, auditable automation that can scale across many devices. A short Python example in this chapter shows the exact sequence for requesting a token, adding it to an X-Auth-Token header, and then calling an endpoint to list network devices. I will point out common pitfalls such as expired tokens, incorrect endpoints, and the lab-only use of disabling TLS verification. By the end of these screens you will be able to authenticate, retrieve inventory data, and describe where provisioning, policy, and assurance APIs fit into an automation workflow. Keep in mind: always test powerful write operations in a lab before applying them in production.

Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Cisco DNA Center & SD-WAN APIs
Cisco DNA Center and SD-WAN Automation APIs
Programmatic control for intent-based campus automation and SD-WAN orchestration.
This chapter teaches token authentication, key API categories, a hands-on Python script to get tokens and list devices, and an introduction to vManage for SD‑WAN automation. Expect code examples, a safety note about TLS in labs, and practical troubleshooting guidance.

screens.title: What is Cisco DNA Center?
screens.narratorSegment: Cisco DNA Center is an automation and assurance platform that shifts network operations from device-by-device configuration to intent-driven policies. In practical terms, intent-based networking means you express high-level outcomes — for example, 'all access switches in Site A should apply the corporate voice QoS profile' — and the controller orchestrates the underlying configuration across many devices. This approach matters because it reduces human error, speeds rollouts, and produces consistent, auditable changes. A concrete example is applying a provisioning template to 20 branch switches: instead of SSH-ing into each device, a single A P I call can push the template and verify completion. A common misconception is that controllers remove the need to understand devices; they do not. You still need to know device roles, interfaces, and templates, but the controller moves repetitive tasks into repeatable APIs. Key takeaways: DNA Center aggregates inventory and assurance data, exposes RESTful APIs for automation, and forms the central point for provisioning and policy workflows. Consider the controller as the single source of truth for high-level network intent while keeping device-level detail available when you need it.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › What is Cisco DNA Center?
Definition and role
DNA Center centralizes network intent, provisioning, and assurance for enterprise networks, providing REST APIs to automate tasks at scale.
Inventory & Discovery
Device discovery and centralized inventory so automation targets are known and consistent.
Provisioning
Apply templates and orchestrate device configuration across many sites.
Assurance
Collect health, telemetry, and performance data for monitoring and closed-loop workflows.
Analogy: orchestral conductor
Like a conductor who directs many musicians to achieve a single piece, DNA Center coordinates devices to achieve a network intent. Each device still plays its part, but the conductor defines the higher-level outcome.
Concrete example
Apply a provisioning template that configures VLANs and QoS across 20 branch switches in a single API call, rather than running identical CLI commands on each device.
Key Takeaway

DNA Center turns high-level intent into coordinated, auditable device actions and exposes APIs for automation at scale.

screens.title: DNA Center API Categories
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the A P I categories is critical for designing automation flows. DNA Center's APIs are grouped to match common operational tasks. Authentication is the first step: request a token so subsequent calls are authorized. Network Discovery finds devices and adds them to inventory, often providing management IPs and hardware details. Provisioning covers templates and push operations that configure devices at scale — use this when onboarding branch routers or applying consistent VLAN and QoS settings. Policy APIs let you express intent such as segmentation or security profiles and apply them across fabrics. Assurance APIs return telemetry, health scores, and troubleshooting data to feed monitoring systems or to close the automation loop. A concrete workflow might authenticate, discover a newly shipped device, apply a provisioning template to configure base settings, attach the device to a site and policy, and then subscribe to assurance metrics to validate successful deployment. A common misconception is that these categories are isolated. In reality they are tightly coupled: provisioning often depends on discovery data, and policy validation relies on assurance telemetry. The clear mental model is: authenticate, discover, provision, apply policy, then assure.

screens.title: DNA Center Authentication: Token Flow
screens.narratorSegment: Authentication is the entry gate for all controller APIs. DNA Center commonly uses token-based authentication: you submit credentials to a specific token endpoint and the controller returns a JSON Web Token that you include in an X-Auth-Token header for later requests. The chapter provides a Python function that performs this request using the requests library and returns the token or None on failure. A concrete example in the code uses a POST to the auth token endpoint with basic HTTP auth and a Content-Type header. Important implementation details include handling exceptions raised by the HTTP client and checking the returned JSON for the token field. A common mistake is assuming tokens last indefinitely; they expire and your automation should detect failure and re-authenticate. Another pitfall is disabling certificate verification in production; the chapter notes disabling TLS verification is only for lab environments. Practice writing the function, run it in a controlled lab, and verify it prints a token. Finally, ensure your script propagates the token to subsequent A P I calls via the X-Auth-Token header so the controller sees those calls as authorized.

keyIdea.text: POST credentials to the auth token endpoint, parse the returned JWT, and include it as X-Auth-Token for API calls; refresh when expired.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › DNA Center Authentication
Concept
Request a token and pass it using the X-Auth-Token header for authorized API access. Handle expiry and errors gracefully.
Python example (excerpt)
import requests

auth_url = f"https://{DNA_CENTER_IP}/dna/system/api/v1/auth/token"
headers = {'Content-Type': 'application/json'}
response = requests.post(auth_url, auth=(USERNAME, PASSWORD), headers=headers, verify=False)
response.raise_for_status()
token = response.json().get('Token')
Practical notes
  • Check for a Token field in the JSON response and return it to callers.
  • Wrap network calls in try-except to handle connectivity and HTTP errors.
  • Detect token expiry by handling 401 responses and re-authenticating as needed.
  • Do not disable TLS verification in production; the chapter warns this is only for lab use.
Common mistake
Assuming tokens never expire or hardcoding the token. Always design for re-authentication and secure credential storage.

The chapter provides a get_network_devices function that builds a GET request to the network-device intent endpoint and includes the X-Auth-Token header. The function calls the endpoint, ensures a successful response, and then inspects the JSON payload for a response array. In practical use, the script iterates over each device and prints the hostname and management IP address. This is useful when you need a programmatic asset list to drive provisioning scripts or monitoring integrations. A concrete example: after calling the endpoint, the script might print lines such as: Hostname: switch-nyc-01, Management IP: 10.1.1.5. A common misconception is that the A P I always returns complete data; in some cases device attributes may be missing if discovery is incomplete, so code should default to 'N/A' for absent fields. Also ensure you handle JSON decode errors and unexpected structures gracefully. Finally, remember that printed output is good for lab verification, while production automation should return structured objects to downstream tasks. content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Listing Network Devices
Code pattern
Call the network-device intent endpoint with the X-Auth-Token header, parse the JSON, and extract hostname and managementIpAddress for each device.
Python snippet
devices_url = f"https://{DNA_CENTER_IP}/dna/intent/api/v1/network-device"
headers = {'X-Auth-Token': auth_token, 'Content-Type': 'application/json'}
response = requests.get(devices_url, headers=headers, verify=False)
response.raise_for_status()
devices_data = response.json()
for device in devices_data.get('response', []):
    name = device.get('hostname', 'N/A')
    mgmt_ip = device.get('managementIpAddress', 'N/A')
    print(f"  - Hostname: {name}, Management IP: {mgmt_ip}")
Practical cautions
  • Guard against missing fields; discovery may be incomplete for some devices.
  • Wrap JSON access in checks and catch JSONDecodeError and RequestException.
  • Use printed output for lab validation; pass structured data in automation pipelines.
Example output
Found 3 devices: - Hostname: switch-nyc-01, Management IP: 10.1.1.5 - Hostname: router-nyc-edge, Management IP: 10.1.1.1

screens.title: Provisioning vs Policy vs Assurance
screens.narratorSegment: Provisioning, policy, and assurance serve distinct but complementary purposes. Provisioning APIs are about creating and applying device configurations; they push templates and set device parameters necessary for a device to function on the network. Policy APIs express intent, such as segmentation or QoS rules, which govern how traffic should be treated or isolated. Assurance APIs provide telemetry and health information that confirms whether provisioning and policy changes achieved the desired outcome. A concrete example: you provision VLANs and interface settings on a new switch, apply a QoS policy to prioritize voice, then query assurance APIs to confirm that voice traffic exhibits the expected performance. A common misconception is that provisioning and policy are the same. They are not — provisioning sets device configuration while policy defines behavioral intent that may be implemented across fabrics. Another mistake is relying solely on provisioning success without checking assurance; without telemetry you cannot be confident the network is meeting the intent. Design automation to provision, then apply policy, then validate via assurance for robust, observable changes. Provisioning vs Policy vs Assurance means provision to configure devices, apply policy to express intent, and use assurance to verify outcomes and close the automation loop.. In practical terms, how these api categories differ and how they work together. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Provisioning vs Policy vs Assurance
Provisioning
Templates, device configuration, and onboarding tasks that set device state.
Example: Push a template to configure VLANs and interface IPs on a new branch switch so it can join the network.
Policy & Assurance
Policy defines desired behavior; assurance reveals whether behavior matches intent using telemetry and health scores.
Example: Apply a segmentation policy to isolate guest traffic, then check assurance APIs for traffic statistics and policy hits to confirm enforcement.
Integration note
Automation should sequence provisioning, policy application, and assurance validation so changes are not only applied but measured and confirmed.

screens.title: Cisco SD-WAN and vManage
screens.narratorSegment: Cisco SD-WAN (Viptela) separates the control and data planes to build an overlay network that is centrally managed. vManage is the centralized management plane that exposes a RESTful A P I surface enabling automated onboarding, template management, policy deployment, and monitoring for the SD‑WAN fabric. This central point is critical because it permits consistent templates and policies to be applied across many edge routers, simplifying large-scale branch operations. A concrete example: you can programmatically create a device template and attach it to a set of edge routers so each device receives identical WAN and security settings. A common misconception is that vManage replaces the need for orchestrating transport — instead, vManage orchestrates the SD‑WAN overlay, while underlying transport remains a separate concern. Another important detail is that vManage returns session cookies (such as JSESSIONID) after authentication; subsequent A P I calls use the cookie rather than a bearer token pattern. Knowing this difference is essential when moving between DNA Center workflows and vManage workflows, because the auth mechanisms and endpoints differ even though both expose RESTful APIs. Cisco SD-WAN and vManage means vmanage centralizes sd‑wan control and exposes apis for onboarding, template and policy management, and monitoring of the entire overlay.. In practical terms, vmanage as the centralized controller for sd-wan automation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: vManage Authentication Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: vManage uses a cookie-based authentication pattern in many deployments. A typical sequence is to POST credentials to the j_security_check endpoint, which responds with a JSESSIONID cookie if authentication succeeds. Subsequent requests include that cookie to maintain the session. The chapter mentions this pattern as the common vManage approach, and it contrasts with DNA Center's token-in-header pattern. A concrete example is using curl to POST to j_security_check, capturing the Set-Cookie header, and then sending that cookie with follow-up curl commands. A common misconception is that cookie-based sessions behave identically to bearer tokens. Cookies represent a server-side session and often have different expiry and reuse semantics; automation must handle session expiration and re-login. Also be mindful of secure cookie handling: protect credentials, use HTTPS, and avoid logging sensitive session cookies. For labs, you might see verify flags to ignore TLS warnings, but in production ensure certificate validation is enabled. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When automating controllers, a few recurring mistakes create the majority of failures. First, expired tokens or sessions: automation must detect 401 responses and re-authenticate rather than failing silently. Second, incorrect endpoints or paths cause errors that can be hard to diagnose; confirm the exact endpoint in controller documentation and log full request metadata in a safe place during development. Third, insufficient user permissions lead to authorization failures even when authentication succeeds; ensure the A P I user has the necessary roles for the actions you intend. Fourth, careless TLS handling: disabling certificate verification may be acceptable in a lab, but doing so in production undermines security. A concrete troubleshooting step is to reproduce the failing A P I call with curl to observe headers and server error messages. Also handle JSON decode errors gracefully and validate response structures before extracting fields. Finally, plan for safety: test write operations in a lab, implement dry-run or simulation modes where possible, and include explicit confirmation steps for high-impact changes. These practices prevent accidental network-wide misconfigurations when automation scales. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will explore two complementary Cisco controllers and their automation APIs: DNA Center, which centers intent-based networking across campus and branch, and vManage, the SD‑WAN controller for overlay automation. We will learn what APIs are available, how token-based authentication works in practice, and how Python scripts can obtain tokens and query device inventories. You will also see how vManage exposes similar automation surfaces for SD‑WAN tasks like onboarding, templates, and monitoring. Understanding these controllers matters because they let you move from repetitive CLI work to repeatable, auditable automation that can scale across many devices. A short Python example in this chapter shows the exact sequence for requesting a token, adding it to an X-Auth-Token header, and then calling an endpoint to list network devices. I will point out common pitfalls such as expired tokens, incorrect endpoints, and the lab-only use of disabling TLS verification. By the end of these screens you will be able to authenticate, retrieve inventory data, and describe where provisioning, policy, and assurance APIs fit into an automation workflow. Keep in mind: always test powerful write operations in a lab before applying them in production.

These are the practical objectives you will meet. First, you will be able to explain DNA Center's role as an intent-based networking controller and how its A P I-driven automation centralizes tasks that would otherwise be manual and device-focused. You will learn concrete examples of that difference, such as applying a network policy that spans many campus switches through a single A P I call. Second, you will explore the main A P I categories: Authentication, Discovery, Provisioning, Policy, and Assurance. For each category you will see what kinds of automation tasks are realistic and why those groupings matter when designing automation workflows. Third, you will authenticate to DNA Center programmatically and write a Python routine that requests a token and then uses it to list devices. The learning target includes parsing a JSON response to extract hostnames and management IPs. Finally, you will be introduced to Cisco SD‑WAN and the vManage A P I so you can describe how templates, onboarding, and monitoring translate into programmatic actions. Each objective ties to hands-on practice and a small competency milestone so you can verify your progress.

Let's restate the chapter objectives with practical checks so you know when you have achieved them. First, being able to explain DNA Center means you can describe a scenario where a single policy change flows to many devices without logging into each switch. A quick check is that you can name one A P I category and an example A P I call within it. Second, for A P I categories you should be able to pick the correct category for a task — for example, provisioning a new branch router uses Provisioning APIs. Third, for the Python authentication objective you will write a function that POSTs credentials, parses the JSON token field, and gracefully handles failures. Run the script in a lab and confirm it prints a token and then prints a list of device hostnames. Fourth, for vManage you should be able to describe the use of a JSESSIONID cookie obtained via j_security_check, and when to prefer controller-level automation versus device-level REST calls. Each objective is tied to a short lab task and one question that verifies understanding.

Cisco DNA Center is an automation and assurance platform that shifts network operations from device-by-device configuration to intent-driven policies. In practical terms, intent-based networking means you express high-level outcomes — for example, 'all access switches in Site A should apply the corporate voice QoS profile' — and the controller orchestrates the underlying configuration across many devices. This approach matters because it reduces human error, speeds rollouts, and produces consistent, auditable changes. A concrete example is applying a provisioning template to 20 branch switches: instead of SSH-ing into each device, a single A P I call can push the template and verify completion. A common misconception is that controllers remove the need to understand devices; they do not. You still need to know device roles, interfaces, and templates, but the controller moves repetitive tasks into repeatable APIs. Key takeaways: DNA Center aggregates inventory and assurance data, exposes RESTful APIs for automation, and forms the central point for provisioning and policy workflows. Consider the controller as the single source of truth for high-level network intent while keeping device-level detail available when you need it.

Understanding the A P I categories is critical for designing automation flows. DNA Center's APIs are grouped to match common operational tasks. Authentication is the first step: request a token so subsequent calls are authorized. Network Discovery finds devices and adds them to inventory, often providing management IPs and hardware details. Provisioning covers templates and push operations that configure devices at scale — use this when onboarding branch routers or applying consistent VLAN and QoS settings. Policy APIs let you express intent such as segmentation or security profiles and apply them across fabrics. Assurance APIs return telemetry, health scores, and troubleshooting data to feed monitoring systems or to close the automation loop. A concrete workflow might authenticate, discover a newly shipped device, apply a provisioning template to configure base settings, attach the device to a site and policy, and then subscribe to assurance metrics to validate successful deployment. A common misconception is that these categories are isolated. In reality they are tightly coupled: provisioning often depends on discovery data, and policy validation relies on assurance telemetry. The clear mental model is: authenticate, discover, provision, apply policy, then assure.

Authentication is the entry gate for all controller APIs. DNA Center commonly uses token-based authentication: you submit credentials to a specific token endpoint and the controller returns a JSON Web Token that you include in an X-Auth-Token header for later requests. The chapter provides a Python function that performs this request using the requests library and returns the token or None on failure. A concrete example in the code uses a POST to the auth token endpoint with basic HTTP auth and a Content-Type header. Important implementation details include handling exceptions raised by the HTTP client and checking the returned JSON for the token field. A common mistake is assuming tokens last indefinitely; they expire and your automation should detect failure and re-authenticate. Another pitfall is disabling certificate verification in production; the chapter notes disabling TLS verification is only for lab environments. Finally, ensure your script propagates the token to subsequent A P I calls via the X-Auth-Token header so the controller sees those calls as authorized.

Provisioning, policy, and assurance serve distinct but complementary purposes. Provisioning APIs are about creating and applying device configurations; they push templates and set device parameters necessary for a device to function on the network. Policy APIs express intent, such as segmentation or QoS rules, which govern how traffic should be treated or isolated. Assurance APIs provide telemetry and health information that confirms whether provisioning and policy changes achieved the desired outcome. A concrete example: you provision VLANs and interface settings on a new switch, apply a QoS policy to prioritize voice, then query assurance APIs to confirm that voice traffic exhibits the expected performance. A common misconception is that provisioning and policy are the same. They are not — provisioning sets device configuration while policy defines behavioral intent that may be implemented across fabrics. Another mistake is relying solely on provisioning success without checking assurance; without telemetry you cannot be confident the network is meeting the intent. Design automation to provision, then apply policy, then validate via assurance for robust, observable changes. vManage uses a cookie-based authentication pattern in many deployments. A typical sequence is to POST credentials to the j_security_check endpoint, which responds with a JSESSIONID cookie if authentication succeeds. Subsequent requests include that cookie to maintain the session. The chapter mentions this pattern as the common vManage approach, and it contrasts with DNA Center's token-in-header pattern. A concrete example is using curl to POST to j_security_check, capturing the Set-Cookie header, and then sending that cookie with follow-up curl commands. A common misconception is that cookie-based sessions behave identically to bearer tokens. Cookies represent a server-side session and often have different expiry and reuse semantics; automation must handle session expiration and re-login. Also be mindful of secure cookie handling: protect credentials, use HTTPS, and avoid logging sensitive session cookies. For labs, you might see verify flags to ignore TLS warnings, but in production ensure certificate validation is enabled. When automating controllers, a few recurring mistakes create the majority of failures. First, expired tokens or sessions: automation must detect 401 responses and re-authenticate rather than failing silently. Second, incorrect endpoints or paths cause errors that can be hard to diagnose; confirm the exact endpoint in controller documentation and log full request metadata in a safe place during development. Third, insufficient user permissions lead to authorization failures even when authentication succeeds; ensure the A P I user has the necessary roles for the actions you intend. Fourth, careless TLS handling: disabling certificate verification may be acceptable in a lab, but doing so in production undermines security. A concrete troubleshooting step is to reproduce the failing A P I call with curl to observe headers and server error messages. Also handle JSON decode errors gracefully and validate response structures before extracting fields. Finally, plan for safety: test write operations in a lab, implement dry-run or simulation modes where possible, and include explicit confirmation steps for high-impact changes. These practices prevent accidental network-wide misconfigurations when automation scales.
